title: Electoral fusion in the United States
wikitext:
{{Short description|Electoral strategy}}

{{distinguish|Fusionism}}
{{Use American English|date=May 2026}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=March 2023}}[[File:Sample ballot from New York's Jefferson County from the 2022 United States election.png|thumb|upright=2.25|An example of an election ballot featuring electoral fusion from the 2022 United States elections in [[Jefferson County, NY]] ]]
{{Voting}}
'''Electoral fusion in the United States''' is an arrangement where two or more [[United States political parties]] on a [[ballot]] list the same [[candidate]],<ref name="auto1">{{Cite magazine |last1=Mitchell |first1=Maurice |last2=Cantor |first2=Dan |date=22 March 2019 |title=In Defense of Fusion Voting |url=https://www.thenation.com/article/archive/fusion-voting-new-york-cuomo-working-families-party/ |magazine=[[The Nation (magazine)|The Nation]] |via=}}</ref> allowing that candidate to receive votes on multiple party lines in the same election.<ref name="business">{{Cite web|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/why-some-candidates-are-listed-twice-on-ballot-2016-11|title=This is why some candidates are listed more than once on your ballot|first=Mark|last=Abadi|website=Business Insider|date=November 8, 2016}}</ref>

Electoral fusion is also known as '''fusion voting''', '''cross endorsement''', '''multiple party nomination''', '''multi-party nomination''', '''plural nomination''' and '''ballot freedom'''.<ref name="What is Fusion">{{cite web|url=http://oregonwfp.org/wp-content/uploads/2010/03/Whatisfusion.pdf |title=What is Fusion |publisher=Oregon Working Families Party |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120415131853/http://oregonwfp.org/wp-content/uploads/2010/03/Whatisfusion.pdf |archive-date=2012-04-15 }}</ref><ref name="Brief for appellant">{{cite web |url=http://www.citizen.org/litigation/article_redirect.cfm?ID=666 |title=Brief for appellant: Twin Cities Area New Party vs Secretary of State of Minnesota |publisher=Public Citizen Foundation}}</ref>

Electoral fusion was once widespread in the U.S. and legal in every state. However, as of 2024, it remains legal and common only in New York and Connecticut.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Realistic Promise of Multiparty Democracy in the United States |url=https://www.newamerica.org/political-reform/reports/the-realistic-promise-of-multiparty-democracy-in-the-united-states/fusion-voting-in-new-york-and-connecticut-an-analysis-of-congressional-races-from-19762022-oscar-pocasangre/ |access-date=2024-10-30 |website=New America |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Fusion Voting and Its Impact on the Upcoming Election |url=https://www.law.com/newyorklawjournal/2024/10/23/fusion-voting-and-its-impact-on-the-upcoming-election/?slreturn=20241030143141 |access-date=2024-10-30 |website=New York Law Journal |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Does Fusion Voting Offer Americans a Way Out of the Partisan Morass? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/11/21/us/politics/fusion-voting-new-jersey.html |website=The New York Times|date=22 November 2022 |last1=Hounshell |first1=Blake }}</ref>

==Overview==
In 2016, ''Business Insider'' wrote: "Fusion voting gives voters a chance to support a major candidate while registering their unhappiness with that candidate's party. A cross-endorsement from a smaller party like the [[Working Families Party (New York)|Working Families Party]] can also help inform voters about where candidates stand on certain issues".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Abadi |first=Mark |title=This is why some candidates are listed more than once on your ballot |url=https://www.businessinsider.com/why-some-candidates-are-listed-twice-on-ballot-2016-11 |access-date=2024-10-30 |website=Business Insider |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2019, ''[[The Nation]]'' wrote: "Fusion is a response to the [[Winner-take-all system|winner-take-all electoral system]]. It solves the '[[wasted vote]]' or '[[Spoiler effect|spoiler]]' dilemmas that otherwise plague [[Third party (U.S. politics)|third parties]], and allows citizens who don't fit neatly into the Democratic or Republican boxes to nevertheless participate constructively in politics".<ref name="auto1"/>

Before the [[American Civil War|Civil War]], fusion voting was a common electoral tactic of [[Abolitionism|abolitionist]] forces, who formed a number of anti-slavery [[Third party (United States)|third parties]], including the [[Liberty Party (United States, 1840)|Liberty]] and [[Free Soil Party|Free Soil]] parties. These and other abolitionist third parties cross-nominated major party candidates running under the [[Whig Party (United States)|Whig]] label, fusing more than one party behind a single candidate.<ref name=":1">{{Cite magazine |last1=Cantor |first1=Daniel |last2=Kristol |first2=William |date=June 15, 2024 |title=What Is "Fusion Voting"? Just a Way to Save the Country, That's All |url=https://newrepublic.com/article/182739/fusion-voting-just-way-save-country-thats |access-date=2024-06-16 |magazine=The New Republic |issn=0028-6583}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Brooks |first=Corey M. |url=https://openlibrary.org/works/OL21109145W/Liberty_Power?edition=key%3A/books/OL28574001M |title=Liberty Power: Anstislavery third Parties and the Transformation of American Politics |publisher=University of Chicago Press |year=2016 |pages=194–204}}</ref>

After the Civil War, agrarian interest groups and the political parties they founded continued to use fusion voting to form alliances between third parties and the weaker of the two major parties, usually the Democrats in the West and Midwest.<ref name=":0" /> In the 19th and early 20th century, minor parties used fusion as a way to signal that their support for a major party candidate brought a meaningful number of voters to the candidate.<ref name="auto">{{Cite journal |last=Eimer |first=S |date=2007 |title=The CIO and third party politics in New York: The rise and fall of the CIO–ALP |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/s0198-8719(06)18004-7 |journal=Political Power and Social Theory |volume=18 |pages=133–171 |doi=10.1016/s0198-8719(06)18004-7 |issn=0198-8719|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Votes for fusion candidates were tallied first by party, then added together to produce the outcome. Historian Peter Argersinger argues that this helped "maintain a significant third party tradition by guaranteeing that dissenters' votes could be more than symbolic protest".<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Argersinger |first=Peter H. |date=April 1980 |title='A Place on the Ballot': Fusion Politics and Antifusion Laws |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/1860557 |journal=The American Historical Review |volume=85 |issue=2 |pages=287–306 |doi=10.2307/1860557 |jstor=1860557 |issn=0002-8762|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Fusion allowed minor parties to avoid the "wasted vote" and "spoiler" dilemmas that small parties face in a non-proportional voting system.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Malinowski |first=Tom |date=6 July 2022 |title=Opinion: A Viable Third Party Is Coming, and It's Starting With a New Jersey Lawsuit |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/07/06/opinion/moderate-party-new-jersey.html?referringSource=articleShare |website=The New York Times}}</ref>

The [[People's Party (United States)|People's Party]] (also known as the Populists) is regarded as the most successful third party of the era.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Argersinger |first=Peter H. |title=The Limits of Agrarian Radicalism: Western Populism and American Politics |publisher=University Press of Kansas |year=1995}}</ref> That success produced a counter-reaction from the dominant major parties, who then used [[State legislature (United States)|state legislatures]] to enact bans against fusion in the late nineteenth and early 20th century.<ref name=":0" /> In northern and western states, fusion was largely banned by [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]]-led legislatures. One Republican [[Minnesota]] state legislator said: "We don't propose to allow the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] to make allies of the Populists, [[Prohibition Party|Prohibitionists]], or any other party, and get up combination tickets against us.  We can whip them single-handed, but don't intend to fight all creation."<ref>{{cite book|title = Spoiling for a Fight: Third-Party Politics in America|pages = 227–228|first = Micah L. |last = Sifry|isbn= 978-0415931434|publisher =Routledge|date =2003}}</ref> In southern states, fusion was largely banned by Democrats who supported [[Jim Crow laws|Jim Crow]], in an attempt to prevent political alliances between [[Black suffrage|newly-enfranchised Black voters]] and poor white farmers.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hunt |first=James L. |date=2006 |title=Fusion of Republicans and Populists |url=https://www.ncpedia.org/fusion-republicans-and-populists |website=Encyclopedia of North Carolina, University of North Carolina Press}}</ref>

Most states banned fusion by the early 20th century.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Tamas |first=Bernard |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ck4PEAAAQBAJ&dq=Most+states+banned+fusion+by+the+early+20th+century&pg=PA79 |title=The Demise and Rebirth of American Third Parties: Poised for Political Revival? |date=2018-03-13 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-351-12825-4 |language=en}}</ref> South Dakota banned the practice in 1999,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sdlegislature.gov/Statutes/Codified_Laws/2040594|title=Codified Law 12-6-3.2 |website=South Dakota Legislature}}</ref> Delaware banned it in 2011,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://legis.delaware.gov/BillDetail/21631|title=Bill Detail - Delaware General Assembly|website=legis.delaware.gov}}</ref> and South Carolina banned it in 2022.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Collins |first=Jeffrey |date=2 March 2022 |title=South Carolina Voting changes unite Democrats, Republicans |work=AP News |url=https://apnews.com/article/2022-midterm-elections-voting-legislature-elections-election-2020-10b999cdf72abd023752048f1da1b528}}</ref> In ''[[Timmons v. Twin Cities Area New Party]]'' (1997), the [[US Supreme Court]] ruled that prohibiting electoral fusion does not violate the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]] of the Constitution.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.law.cornell.edu/supct/html/95-1608.ZS.html| title=Timmons v. Twin Cities Area New Party (95–1608), 520 U.S. 351 (1997)| publisher=Legal Information Institute/Cornell| access-date=4 January 2015}}</ref>

Electoral fusion was once widespread in the US, but as of 2024, it remains legal and common only in New York and [[Connecticut]].<ref name=":1" /> It is partially legal in three other states: California allows fusion in presidential elections only, and [[Pennsylvania]] and [[Maryland]] permit it in certain elections, including but not limited to the [[judiciary]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Cobble |first1=Steve |title=Fusion: Multiple Party Nomination in the United States |last2=Siskind |first2=Sarah |publisher=Center for a New Democracy at the Tides Foundation |year=1993 |location=San Francisco}}</ref>{{Page needed|date=October 2023}} In Oregon and Vermont, a system of dual-labeling exists, which allows a candidate to list multiple party endorsements on a single line, but disallows the traditional fusion system in which a minor party has its own ballot line and votes are tallied by party.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Adams |first=Terrence |date=16 January 2013 |title=Cross-Endorsing Candidates |url=https://www.cga.ct.gov/2013/rpt/2013-R-0046.htm |access-date=25 February 2023 |website=Connecticut General Assembly Office of Legislative Research}}</ref> In [[New Hampshire]], fusion is legal in rare cases when primary elections are won by [[write-in candidate]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Greene |first=Rick |date=17 October 2022 |title=Your ballot might list the same candidate under two parties. That's allowed under N.H. law. |url=https://www.nhpr.org/politics/2022-10-17/new-hampshire-ballot-candidates-multiple-parties-elections-democrat-libertarian-republican-hillsborough-county |website=New Hampshire Public Radio}}</ref>

As of 2024, the [[Alianza de País]] in Puerto Rico, the [[Moderate Party (New Jersey)|New Jersey Moderate Party]], the Common Sense Party in Michigan and the [[United Kansas]] Party are attempting to use litigation to bring back fusion voting in their areas.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Hounshell |first=Blake |date=21 November 2022 |title=Does Fusion Voting Offer Americans a Way Out of the Partisan Morass? |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/11/21/us/politics/fusion-voting-new-jersey.html |access-date=25 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.primerahora.com/noticias/gobierno-politica/notas/dalmau-cataloga-candidatura-de-medico-a-comisionado-residente-como-un-acto-de-generosidad-y-desprendimiento/|title=Dalmau cataloga candidatura de médico a comisionado residente como 'un acto de generosidad y desprendimiento' |lang=es-PR|author-first1= Osman |author-last1=Pérez Méndez|date=2 January 2024|access-date=26 July 2024|work=[[Primera Hora (Puerto Rico)|Primera Hora]]}}</ref>

[[New Mexico]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Metzger |first=Bryan |date=2021-03-09 |title=Independent voters surpass 20 percent, but lack representation. Lawmakers unswayed. |url=https://nmindepth.com/2021/independent-voters-surpass-20-percent-but-lack-representation-lawmakers-unswayed/ |access-date=2025-03-02 |website=New Mexico In Depth |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Massachusetts]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bill S.424 |url=https://malegislature.gov/Bills/193/S424 |access-date=2025-03-02 |website=malegislature.gov}}</ref> and [[Rhode Island]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=H5712 |url=https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/Billtext/BillText25/HouseText25/H5712.htm |access-date=2025-03-02 |website=webserver.rilegislature.gov}}</ref> had bills to allow fusion voting.

== Historical examples ==
===Presidential elections===
In [[1872 United States presidential election|1872]], both the newly formed [[Liberal Republican Party (United States)|Liberal Republican Party]] and the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] nominated the Liberal Republican [[Horace Greeley]] as their candidate for US President: "If [the Democratic Party] was to stand any chance at all against Grant, it must avoid putting up a candidate of its own who would merely split the opposition vote. It must take Greeley."<ref>Hale, William Harlan (1950). Horace Greeley: Voice of the People. Harper & Brothers. {{OCLC|336934}}. p. 338</ref>

In the [[1896 United States presidential election|presidential election of 1896]], [[William Jennings Bryan]] was nominated by both the Democratic Party and the [[People's Party (United States)|Populist Party]], albeit with different vice presidential candidates, [[Arthur Sewall]] for the Democrats and [[Thomas E. Watson]] for the Populists. This election led to the downfall of the Populist Party, especially in Southern states (such as Watson's Georgia, as well as North Carolina and Tennessee) where the Populist party had engaged in electoral fusion or other alliances with Republicans against the dominant [[Bourbon Democrat]]s.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://history.missouristate.edu/wrmiller/Populism/Texts/Documents/Bibliography/african_American.htm |title=African |publisher=History.missouristate.edu |access-date=2 July 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100307005107/http://history.missouristate.edu/wrmiller/Populism/texts/Documents/Bibliography/african_American.htm |archive-date=7 March 2010 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=9 November 1894 |title=Senate and House Secured; Republican control in the next Congress assured. The House of Representatives Republican by More than Two – thirds Majority – Possible Loss of a Republican Senator from the State of Washington – Republicans and Populists Will Organize the Senate and Divide the Patronage |url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=9A00E7DF1231E033A2575AC0A9679D94659ED7CF |access-date=26 May 2010 |work=The New York Times}}</ref>

In the [[1936 United States presidential election|1936]] and [[1940 United States presidential election|1940]], the [[American Labor Party]] nominated [[Franklin D. Roosevelt|Franklin Roosevelt]] for president, and in [[1944 United States presidential election|1944]], the [[Liberal Party of New York]] cross-nominated Roosevelt, fusing with the ALP.  Roosevelt won the state of New York in each election, but in 1940 and 1944 he would not have won New York without the support of votes gained via the fusion parties and their voters.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Soyer |first=Daniel |title=Left in the Center: The Liberal Party of New York and the Rise and Fall of American Social Democracy |publisher=Cornell University Press |year=2022}}</ref>

[[Donald Trump]] appeared on the [[2016 United States presidential election in California|2016 presidential ballot in California]] with two ballot labels by his name,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Winger |first=Richard |date=2016-08-13 |title=American Independent Party Formally Nominates Donald Trump and Michael Pence |url=http://ballot-access.org/2016/08/13/american-independent-party-formally-nominates-donald-trump-and-michael-pence/ |access-date=2024-08-31 |website=ballot-access.org |language=en-US}}</ref> as the nominee of both the Republican Party and the [[American Independent Party]], a small far-right party. Trump was the first fusion presidential candidate on the California ballot in at least eighty years.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-08-16 |title=Donald Trump will be the nominee of two parties on California's November ballot |url=https://www.latimes.com/politics/la-pol-ca-donald-trump-california-ballot-american-independent-party-20160815-snap-story.html |access-date=2024-08-31 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Connecticut ===
Connecticut allows cross-endorsements, listing candidates on more than one ballot line. Minor parties include the [[Working Families Party]] and [[Independent Party of Connecticut|Independent Party]]. In 2010, [[Dannel Malloy]] won the gubernatorial election within the [[Working Families]]' margin.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pazniokas |first=Mark |date=2024-11-04 |title=CT 2024 election: Your legislator is on 2 or 3 ballot lines. Why? |url=https://ctmirror.org/2024/11/04/ct-ballot-lines/ |access-date=2025-03-01 |website=CT Mirror |language=en-US}}</ref>

===New York===
{{See also|Elections in New York (state)|Qualified New York political parties}}

In 1936, labor leaders in New York City took advantage of fusion and founded the American Labor Party (ALP). Their immediate goal was to provide a way for New Yorkers who despised the [[Tammany Hall]] political machine to support Franklin Roosevelt without voting for the Democratic Party. In its first showing at the polls, the party garnered a significant amount of the vote in New York City but was not important with regard to Roosevelt's victory. In the 1937 election cycle, the ALP built on its past performance by electing members to the city council, and by delivering so many votes to Mayor [[Fiorello La Guardia]] that the ''New York Times'' ran a front page article declaring that the ALP held the balance of power in city and state politics. The importance of the ALP was demonstrated again in 1938 when the party provided the margin of victory for the Democratic candidate for Governor, and in 1940 when the ALP did the same for President Roosevelt.  In the 1944 presidential election, fusion provided [[Congress of Industrial Organizations|CIO]] unions in New York an opportunity to build and back a labor party, an uncommon occurrence in the US. Labor leaders knew that fusion permitted them to field candidates and win elections on the American Labor Party line in local elections, and to back Democrats in statewide or national races where they did not have the capacity to field successful candidates. Given the presence of fusion in New York, the Greater New York Industrial Union Council (GNYIUC), the CIO's local labor federation in New York, formally affiliated with the party making it the political arm of the New York CIO. This relationship would continue until 1948 when the GNYIUC opted to back [[Henry A. Wallace|Henry Wallace]] for president, instead of using fusion to back President Truman. This led to internal conflicts within the CIO and ultimately contributed to the decision by the national CIO to revoke the charter of the GNYIUC, thereby ending its relationship with the ALP.<ref name="auto"/>

As of 2023, to obtain or maintain automatic ballot access, a party's candidate for [[Governor of New York|Governor]] in [[United States midterm election|midterm election]] years or [[President of the United States|President]] in presidential years must receive either 130,000 votes or 2% of votes cast (whichever is greater) on that party's line.<ref>{{cite web |title=Ballot access requirements for political parties in New York |url=https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_New_York |website=Ballotpedia |language=en}}</ref>

Other parties, such as the [[Libertarian Party of New York]] and the [[Green Party of New York]], have sought ballot access by first getting a gubernatorial candidate on the ballot via [[petition]] (by collecting 45,000 valid signatures of [[registered voters]]), and then by getting 130,000 votes for that candidate on their line. As a general rule, neither party uses electoral fusion, and both rely on their own candidates. The Green Party, which had first achieved ballot status in 1998, failed to gain 50,000 votes (then the requirement) and also lost its ballot status in 2002, but regained its line when the 2010 election results were certified. In 2018, [[Larry Sharpe (political activist)|Larry Sharpe]], the Libertarian Party candidate for governor in New York, received over 90,000 votes, giving the party ballot status for the first time in its history.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://nyenr.elections.ny.gov/ |title=NYS Board of Elections Unofficial Election Night Results |access-date=2019-01-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181120174014/https://nyenr.elections.ny.gov/ |archive-date=2018-11-20 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Welch |first=Matt |date=2018-10-31 |title=Libertarian Larry Sharpe Has Raised a Record $450,000 in New York Governor's Race |url=https://reason.com/2018/10/31/libertarian-larry-sharpe-has-raised-a-re/ |access-date=2024-10-30 |website=Reason.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Larry Sharpe Is Libertarian Candidate For Governor - Sanctuary For Independent Media |url=https://www.mediasanctuary.org/stories/2022/larry-sharpe-is-libertarian-candidate-for-governor/ |access-date=2024-10-30}}</ref>

In July 2019, the [[New York Legislature]] passed a budget bill that included the creation of a Public Campaign Financing Commission, which was given authority to investigate and create rules for [[public financing of campaigns]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.governor.ny.gov/news/governor-cuomo-legislative-leaders-announce-members-public-campaign-financing-commission|title=Governor Cuomo & Legislative Leaders Announce Members of the Public Campaign Financing Commission|date=3 July 2019|website=Governor Andrew M. Cuomo|access-date=2 August 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190802172540/https://www.governor.ny.gov/news/governor-cuomo-legislative-leaders-announce-members-public-campaign-financing-commission|archive-date=2 August 2019|url-status=dead}}</ref> The [[Conservative Party of New York]] and the [[Working Families Party]] each filed lawsuits against the state in response, alleging that the commission was a disguised attempt to end fusion voting and thus the existence of New York's third parties.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/07/23/nyregion/fusion-voting-lawsuit.html|title=2 Opposing Political Parties, Fighting for Survival, Sue Cuomo|first=Jesse|last=McKinley|newspaper=The New York Times |date=23 July 2019}}</ref>

The [[2021 New York City Democratic mayoral primary]] was the city's first mayoral primary to implement [[Instant-runoff voting|ranked-choice voting]], allowing voters to rank up to five candidates.<ref>{{cite web |date=January 6, 2021 |title=Ranked-Choice Voting: What It Is And What We Need To Do As A Community |url=https://www.queensjewishlink.com/index.php/local/26-community-corner/3809-ranked-choice-voting-what-it-is-and-what-we-need-to-do-as-a-community |publisher=Queens Jewish Link}}</ref> In the [[2025 New York City Democratic mayoral primary|2025 Democratic mayoral primary]], [[Brad Lander]] and eventual nominee [[Zohran Mamdani|Zohran Mandani]] cross-endorsed each other for second place.<ref name="LanderMamdani">{{cite web |last=Ngo |first=Emily |date=June 13, 2025 |title=Zohran Mamdani, Brad Lander are cross-endorsing in race for New York City mayor |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2025/06/13/mamdani-lander-cross-endorsing-mayor-00405357 |access-date=June 13, 2025 |website=[[Politico]]}}</ref> Mamdani would also cross-endorse with [[Michael Blake (politician)|Michael Blake]] a few days later.<ref name="BlakeMamdani">{{cite web |last=Fitzsimmons |first=Emma |date=June 16, 2025 |title=Mamdani and Blake Will Cross-Endorse in N.Y.C. Mayor's Race |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/06/16/nyregion/mamdani-blake-nyc-mayors-race.html |access-date=June 16, 2025 |website=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> In [[2025 New York City mayoral election|the general election]], Mamdani would appear on the ballot both as the Democratic candidate and the candidate for the [[Working Families Party]].<ref name="wfp">{{Cite web |date=May 31, 2025 |title=Working Families Party ranks Zohran Mamdani as top pick for mayor |url=https://ny1.com/nyc/all-boroughs/politics/2025/05/31/working-families-party-ranks-zohran-mamdani-as-top-pick-for-mayor |website=ny1.com}}</ref> Due to the votes from Working Families, Mamdani reached a majority in the first round.

===Oregon===
Prior to 1958, Oregon practiced a form of fusion that required the state to list multiple nominating parties on the candidate's ballot line. [[Sylvester Pennoyer]] was elected governor in 1886 and 1890 as a candidate of the Democratic and People's parties.  In 1906, seven members of the Oregon House were also elected as candidates of the [[People's Party (United States)|People's Party]] and either the Democratic or Republican parties.  In 2008, a lawsuit was brought by the [[Independent Party of Oregon]] against the Oregon Secretary of State claiming that modifications to the ballot design statute in 1995 once again required the state to list multiple nominating parties on the candidate's ballot line. The lawsuit gave rise to legislation<ref name="SB326">{{Cite web |title=SB326 2009 Regular Session |url=https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2009R1/Error |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201027221816/https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2009R1/Measures/Overview/SB326 |archive-date=2020-10-27 |access-date=2024-10-26 |website=Oregon Legislative Information System}}</ref>{{Secondary source needed|date=August 2024}} to allow candidates to list up to three party labels after their name.  This bill passed both houses of the Oregon legislature during the 2009 legislative session. Governor [[Ted Kulongoski]] signed the bill into law on 23 July 2009.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tracking Senate Bill 326 in the Oregon Legislature |url=https://gov.oregonlive.com/bill/2009/SB326/ |access-date=2025-03-01 |website=Your Government :: The Oregonian |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Pennsylvania===
In Pennsylvania, fusion can occur when members of a party write in the name of a member of a different party in a primary election and secure enough write-in votes to nominate that party's candidate.  For example, if Bob Jones is running for school board in a primary election as a Democrat and secures both enough votes from members of his own party as well as enough write-in votes from members of the Republican Party, then electoral fusion occurs, and Bob will appear on the ballot as both a Republican and a Democrat. Similarly, a member of one party may lose their own party's nomination in a primary election but gain enough write-in votes from members of the opposing party to win that party's nomination.  For example, in May 2023, [[Stephen Zappala]] lost the Democratic primary for [[Allegheny County District Attorney]] to challenger Matt Dugan. However, although Zappala is a Democrat, he received the requisite number (500 or more) of write-in votes from Republicans to appear as a Republican on the ballot in November 2023.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Lyons |first1=Kim |date=19 May 2023 |title='Halftime?' Allegheny Co. Dem DA nominee Dugan may face Zappala again in November |url=https://www.penncapital-star.com/campaigns-elections/halftime-allegheny-co-dem-da-nominee-dugan-may-face-zappala-again-in-november/ |access-date=May 20, 2023 |website=[[Pennsylvania Capital-Star]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=23 May 2023 |title=Zappala receives enough write-in votes to run as Republican |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/pittsburgh/news/stephen-zappala-republican-write-in-votes/ |access-date=25 May 2023 |website=[[CBS News]]}}</ref> Running on the ballot as a Republican, Zappala won the general election in November 2023, beating Dugan.

=== Vermont ===
In Vermont, candidates can only run in one party primary, but can run write-in campaigns in others. Political science professor Jack Gierzynski said "When parties work together in a fusion sense, they're much more likely to be successful. ... [Progressives] running on a fusion ticket has had a big influence on moving the public policy needle to the left."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cutler |first=Calvin |date=2022-08-25 |title=Three Vt. Democratic primary winners to run as fusion candidates |url=https://www.wcax.com/2022/08/25/three-vt-democratic-primary-winners-run-fusion-candidates/ |access-date=2025-03-01 |website=WCAX |language=en}}</ref>

Fusion voting had been at risk due to a [[Sore loser law|sore loser]] provision of [[ranked-choice voting]] legislation.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Viglienzoni |first=Cat |date=2023-06-15 |title=Vt. election reform bill could be taken up in veto session |url=https://www.wcax.com/2023/06/15/vt-election-reform-bill-could-be-taken-up-veto-session/ |access-date=2025-03-01 |website=WCAX |language=en}}</ref>

===Wisconsin===
In [[Milwaukee]], [[Wisconsin]], during the heyday of the [[Sewer socialism|sewer socialists]], the Republican and Democratic parties would agree not to run candidates against each other in some districts, concentrating instead on defeating the socialists. These candidates were usually called [[non-partisan]], but sometimes were termed fusion candidates instead.<ref>"Fusion In Many Districts; Old Parties Unite On Legislative Candidates" ''[[Milwaukee Journal]]'' 1 November 1918; p. 9, col. 2</ref>{{Additional citation needed|date=August 2024}}

extract:
Electoral fusion in the United States is an arrangement where two or more United States political parties on a ballot list the same candidate, allowing that candidate to receive votes on multiple party lines in the same election.
Electoral fusion is also known as fusion voting, cross endorsement, multiple party nomination, multi-party nomination, plural nomination and ballot freedom.
Electoral fusion was once widespread in the U.S. and legal in every state. However, as of 2024, it remains legal and common only in New York and Connecticut.
